claim: Rajasthan Foundation places Jodhpur district within its Marwar region listing.
evidence_summary: The page enumerates Jaisalmer, Barmer, and Jodhpur districts under Marwar and lists Jodhpur among its towns/cities.
notes: Geographic context only; this does not define a single uniform Marwari identity.

claim: The Rajasthan Foundation lists Marwari among the varieties/dialects of Rajasthani.
evidence_summary: The institutional page names Marwari, Mewari, Dundari, and Vagadi as examples under its Rajasthani-language overview.
notes: The page does not establish fine-grained Jodhpur speech patterns or provide validated phrases.

claim: Rajasthan Tourism describes Mehrangarh Fort as dominating a rocky ridge above Jodhpur and describes blue-toned buildings in the city.
evidence_summary: The Jodhpur page calls it the Blue City and describes blue shades on forts, palaces, temples, havelis, houses, and the fort's rocky ridge setting.
notes: A destination description; not a claim that all homes are blue or representative of rural Marwar.

claim: A Rajasthan Tourism account of the Marwar Festival in Jodhpur presents Jodhpuri safas and bandhini dupattas as festival clothing.
evidence_summary: The travel diary describes festival displays at Mehrangarh Fort and Umaid Bhawan featuring traditional attire including Jodhpuri safas (turbans) and bandhini tie-dye dupattas.
notes: Festival presentation evidence; it does not establish everyday or universal clothing.
source_title: Discovering an All New Side of the Heritage of Jodhpur

claim: Rajasthan Tourism lists tie-and-dye bandhej fabrics among textiles associated with Jodhpur.
evidence_summary: The official shopping guide names Jodhpur, Jaipur, and Bikaner for tie-and-dye bandhej fabrics.
notes: Craft/location association; no claim about who wears a particular textile or on what occasion.

claim: Rajasthan Tourism identifies Salawas village near Jodhpur with dhurries made using cotton yarn or camel hair.
evidence_summary: The shopping guide names Salawas in Jodhpur among places to buy dhurries and describes village-made rugs with geometric or floral patterns.
notes: This supports a named craft/product, not its presence in every home.

claim: Rajasthan Tourism describes Osian near Jodhpur with temple ruins, a stepwell, and a camel-ride/sunset viewpoint.
evidence_summary: The Jodhpur destination page locates Osian about 65 km from Jodhpur and describes a stepwell, temple ruins, and a rustic camel-ride and sunset setting.
notes: Visitor-facing description of Osian; it does not define all rural landscapes in Marwar.

claim: Rajasthan Tourism says Khejri trees are prominent in western Rajasthan and identifies Khejrli village near Jodhpur with the tree's name.
evidence_summary: The Jodhpur page connects the village name Khejrli to Khejri (Prosopis cineraria), described there as prominent in western Rajasthan.
notes: The source is about one village and a regional tree; it does not establish a complete rural ecology profile.

claim: Rajasthan Tourism describes the Marwar Festival in Jodhpur as featuring folk music and songs honoring former rulers of Marwar.
evidence_summary: The Jodhpur page says the festival features folk music and art forms revisiting stories written and sung to honor former Marwar rulers.
notes: Festival and commemorative performance context; not a general claim about everyday music.

claim: Rajasthan Tourism describes Ghoomar performances at Mandore Garden during its Marwar Festival account.
evidence_summary: The official travel diary identifies Ghoomar as a featured performance at Mandore Garden in its description of the Jodhpur festival.
notes: Event-specific evidence; not a claim about all Marwari communities or occasions.
source_title: Discovering an All New Side of the Heritage of Jodhpur

claim: Rajasthan Tourism describes Toran-Bandan as a wedding custom in which a mounted groom touches a floral decoration over the bride's doorway.
evidence_summary: The statewide customs page describes the groom approaching on horseback, touching the toran above the entrance, and being greeted by his mother-in-law with tilak.
notes: Not independently established here as a specifically Marwari or Jodhpur practice.

claim: Rajasthan Foundation lists bajra, gram flour, corn, barley, and dairy products among common ingredients in Rajasthan cuisine.
evidence_summary: The Foundation's statewide cuisine overview relates listed ingredients to regional availability and notes dal baati churma, ker sangri, and other dishes as examples of Rajasthani cuisine.
notes: Statewide overview only; do not infer a particular Marwari household menu or dietary practice.

claim: The study records daily-wear traditional garments for surveyed Sindhi-Sepahi Musalman Rajput men (safa, kurta, bandi, lungi) and women (odhana, kurati, kanchli, ghaghra, sarara).
evidence_summary: The 2005–2006 study surveyed 168 villages across seven Jodhpur-district tehsils; the garment list is reported for this named community, not for Marwari people generally.
notes: Directly supports the study’s reported list for the sampled community and period. Ravi and Meena have no stated community identity; do not apply to them without establishing relevant community and scene context. Not evidence of present-day prevalence.
scope: Sindhi-Sepahi Musalman Rajput community; daily wear recorded in a 2005–2006 survey in Jodhpur district
source_title: Traditional Costumes of Musalman Rajput Community in Western Rajasthan, India

claim: The Mehrangarh Museum Trust catalogues early-20th-century paag (turban) cloths from Jodhpur as “Paags of Marwar” and describes paag styles and associations with social groups, seasons, rituals, ceremonies, moods and emotions.
evidence_summary: The museum catalogue describes paag as a men’s headdress, calls it a symbol of pride and valor in Marwar, notes distinct tying styles among Marwar social groups, and describes color/pattern associations, including leheriya with the rainy season.
notes: Evidence for the catalogued objects and museum’s stated interpretation. Styles vary by social group; the page does not establish a paag for an unknown character or establish this as the character’s scene-specific everyday dress.
scope: Marwar-specific; early-20th-century museum collection from Jodhpur; catalogue-described group and seasonal/ritual associations

claim: The Mehrangarh Museum Trust identifies a Jodhpur poshak as a 20th-century women’s ensemble and states that Jodhpur royals adopted its present form in the late 19th or early 20th century.
evidence_summary: The catalogue describes the ensemble’s components and explicitly locates the adoption of its present form among Jodhpur royals.
notes: Historical royal-context evidence only. It does not establish ordinary rural clothing or apply to Meena absent a matching character, period and context.
scope: Jodhpur royal women; 20th-century ensemble; late-19th/early-20th-century royal adoption

claim: The Mehrangarh Museum Trust describes the jama as adopted by Jodhpur’s rulers and says that in 19th-century Marwar it grew in length and flare into ankle-length robes.
evidence_summary: The catalogue entry concerns an early-19th-century block-printed cotton jama and places its development in Mughal/Jodhpur court dress; this specimen is described as likely from Maharaja Man Singh’s time.
notes: Historical court evidence only. It does not support ordinary rural clothing for Ravi or any present-day scene.
scope: Marwar royal/court clothing; 19th century; museum object
